name: Pioneer Square
label: Pioneer Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'James Street and Yesler Way' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of James Street and Yesler Way (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3388921: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic district with Romanesque brick buildings and the pergola.

text.description: Pioneer Square is a neighbourhood in the southwest corner of downtown Seattle, once the heart of the city, and it is named after a small triangular plaza near First Avenue and Yesler Way, once called Pioneer Place. Seattle's founders settled here in 1852. Most of the early wooden buildings burned in the Great Seattle Fire of 1889, and by the end of 1890 dozens of brick and stone buildings had replaced them. Those late 19th-century buildings, mostly in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, still give the neighbourhood its look, and the area is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as a historic district. That mix of dark brick, old ironwork and street corners is what makes it good for phone photos. From here Smith Tower rises behind the parking garage known as the sinking ship. It is a good place for a wide, street-level shot with the whole scene in one frame, and it works especially well after rain, when puddles reflect the tower and buildings. If you want the classic view of the cast-iron pergola, with the totem pole and brick buildings around it, walk on to Pioneer Place Park. Occidental Park is the one for Smith Tower above the brick buildings. Keep an eye on your phone and your surroundings while you frame your shots.
text.geographic_location: Pioneer Square is in the southwest corner of downtown Seattle, a short way inland from the Elliott Bay waterfront.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops close to this spot, so head for the Pioneer Square neighbourhood in the southwest corner of downtown Seattle. From there, the little triangular plaza is east, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so Smith Tower, the parking garage and the street all fit in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter, calmer shot, or the telephoto if your phone has one (2x-5x) to pick out the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of James Street and Yesler Way (corner near the parking garage known as the sinking ship). Smith Tower rising behind the parking garage, with a wide-angle view that works especially well when puddles reflect the scene after rain. Stand on James Street and Yesler Way, at the corner near the parking garage known as the sinking ship. From here Smith Tower rises behind the garage. The small plaza and the pergola are a short walk to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines. Keep the phone level so the tall building does not lean. After rain, hold the phone low over a puddle so the tower and buildings reflect in it. For the classic pergola shot, walk on to Pioneer Place Park. Occidental Park is the one for Smith Tower above the brick buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If the reflection is the subject, tap on the puddle instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just after rain, when puddles have formed, is the best time for the reflection shot. Golden hour suits the view of Smith Tower above the brick buildings in Occidental Park.

text.access_note: This is an open city street corner and public square, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any nearby attraction, such as the Smith Tower observation deck, which is paid.

name: Space Needle
label: Space Needle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kerry Park' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kerry Park' (way/49734702): middle (99 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/12903132: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Space Needle' (53 m across).

text.description:
The Space Needle is Seattle's best-known tower, built for the 1962 World's Fair, which drew more than 2.3 million visitors. It stands 605 ft (184 m) tall, and its flying-saucer top sits on a slim, hourglass-shaped frame. When it was finished it was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River. Skyscrapers have since overtaken it.

The classic phone photo is taken from Kerry Park, the hilltop park on Queen Anne. From the south-facing overlook railing, the Needle sits in the middle of the skyline. Elliott Bay lies alongside, and on clear days Mount Rainier shows behind. The park is small, so it can get busy before sunset. Arrive early to claim a spot at the railing.

Two alternatives are worth knowing. At Volunteer Park the Needle can appear centred inside the Black Sun sculpture, or over the reflecting pond, but it is far away, so you will want your telephoto lens. At Olympic Sculpture Park the red steel sculpture The Eagle makes a foreground, with the Needle rising behind.

The mountain only appears when the sky is clear, so check the weather before you climb the hill. Keep the Needle's slim shape upright in the frame, and leave some sky above it.
text.geographic_location: The Space Needle is in the Lower Queen Anne neighbourhood, inside Seattle Center, next to the downtown skyline. The Kerry Park viewpoint is on the hill of Queen Anne, to the north-west of the tower.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so start from Lower Queen Anne or Seattle Center (the Needle is at 400 Broad Street) and head north-west up the Queen Anne hill to Kerry Park. Parking at the park is on the street and can be hard to find, so walking up is often easier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole skyline, bay and Needle together. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the Needle with Mount Rainier behind it. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the Needle look small, so use it only for a scene-setting shot with the park railing and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kerry Park (south-facing overlook railing). The Space Needle sits in the middle of the downtown skyline, with Elliott Bay alongside and Mount Rainier behind on clear days. From here you look out over downtown, with the Space Needle in the middle of the skyline, Elliott Bay alongside and Mount Rainier behind on clear days.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the Needle on one of the vertical lines so the tower stays upright. Leave a little sky above the saucer. Include a strip of the railing or city rooftops in the foreground for depth. If you have time, Volunteer Park (Needle centred in the Black Sun sculpture, from far away) and Olympic Sculpture Park (The Eagle in the foreground, Needle behind) give different views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Needle to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the buildings are not washed out. At blue hour, try night mode and rest your phone on the railing to keep it still. Take a Live Photo too, in case people move through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or blue hour gives the best light for this view. Arrive early, as the park fills up before sunset. Mount Rainier only shows when the sky is clear, so check the forecast.

text.access_note: Kerry Park is an open public park and free to enter; if you plan to go up the Space Needle itself, check the official site before you go.

label: Pike Place Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Public Market Center' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of 1st Avenue and Pine Street (our map tiles).

text.description: Pike Place Market is a public market on the western edge of Downtown Seattle, looking out over Elliott Bay. It opened on 17 August 1907 and is one of the older continuously operated public farmers' markets in the United States. It is also Seattle's most popular tourist destination, with more than 20 million visitors a year. The classic photo here is the red neon Public Market Center sign and clock, shot head-on with the market entrance and street life behind it. Because the sign sits at the bottom of a slope, standing uphill gives a cleaner view than standing right under it. The market is built on the edge of a steep hill, with the covered arcades on the upper street level selling fish, fresh produce and crafts, and more shops on lower levels below. If you want a calmer view, try Pike Street for a street scene with Puget Sound behind it, or MarketFront for wide views over Elliott Bay and the Great Wheel. It gets very busy at the sign, so go early if you can, and keep an eye on the traffic.
text.geographic_location: Pike Place Market sits roughly in the north-west corner of Downtown Seattle's central business district, with Belltown to the north and the waterfront and Elliott Bay to the south-west. Its main street, Pike Place, runs north-west from Pike Street to Virginia Street.
text.directions_text: From Downtown Seattle, the market is on the western side of the centre, by the waterfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the sign head-on. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or crowds stop you stepping back, or if you want more street and sky. Try 2x to pull the sign closer without walking into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of 1st Avenue and Pine Street (center of the crosswalk, uphill from the sign). The red neon Public Market Center sign and clock framed head-on, with the market entrance and street traffic behind. Use the uphill crosswalk near the Public Market Center sign. From here the red neon sign and clock face you directly, with the market entrance and street traffic behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the sign in the middle, with the clock level against a horizontal line. Include a little of the street and market entrance behind it to show where you are. For a different view, Pike Street gives a quieter street scene with Puget Sound behind, and MarketFront looks wide over Elliott Bay and the Great Wheel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the red neon keeps its colour instead of washing out. Take a few shots, as people and vehicles will keep moving through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the usual advice, because the crowds at the sign are heavy later in the day. Views of Mount Rainier and the Olympics from MarketFront depend on clear weather.

text.access_note: The market is a working public market with streets and arcades that visitors walk through, but individual shops and stalls keep their own times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Gum Wall
label: Gum Wall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gum Wall' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

notes: Alley wall covered in chewing gum next to Pike Place Market.

text.description: The Gum Wall is a brick wall in Post Alley, beneath Pike Place Market, covered in layers of used chewing gum in every colour. It began by accident in the 1990s, when patrons of shows at the Market Theater started sticking gum to the walls. The market's officials eventually decided to let it stay, and it became a local landmark. It is about 54 feet (16 m) long and 8 feet (2.4 m) high as of 2024. It has been steam-cleaned several times, most recently in November 2024, so how much gum you see changes over time. That makes it a good subject for a phone: the wall is bright, textured and full of small details such as love messages and little artworks. Stand right in front of the wall, beside the Market Theater box office, and frame it head-on so the pattern fills the picture. This also leaves room for a friend or partner to pose, which is why wedding photographers like it too. Then move in close for a detail shot of a few bricks. The alley is narrow, so wait a moment for a gap in the passers-by. Please don't touch the wall, and don't let children or bags lean on it. If you want some context, step back to Post Alley for a wider view of the gum-covered walls and the market area.
text.geographic_location: The Gum Wall is in Post Alley, beneath Pike Place Market in downtown Seattle, near Pike Street. It sits just south of the market's main entrance off 1st Avenue, beside the Market Theater box office.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Pike Place Market and its main entrance off 1st Avenue. The Gum Wall is just south of there, down in Post Alley near Pike Street. Walk from the market to reach it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the head-on view of the wall with a person in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the alley is too tight to fit what you want. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of single bricks and small gum shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The wall is at the point itself, so you are standing at the subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Face the wall straight on so the gum mosaic fills the frame, and leave room for a person posing in front. Turn on gridlines and line them up with the brick courses to keep the picture level. For a wider alternative, step back along Post Alley to show the gum-covered walls with the market entrance area and passers-by behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the brightest gum looks washed out. Portrait mode can work for a person posing, but check that the edges of their hair and clothes look clean against the busy background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when there are usually fewer people in the background. Summer afternoons and weekends are the busiest.

text.access_note: The Gum Wall is in an open-air public alley by Pike Place Market; opening hours may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chihuly Garden and Glass
label: Chihuly Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chihuly Garden and Glass' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

notes: Glass art exhibition and garden below the Space Needle.

text.description: Chihuly Garden and Glass sits in Seattle Center, right beside the Space Needle, and shows the studio glass of Dale Chihuly. It opened on 21 May 2012 on the site of the old Fun Forest amusement park. There are three main parts: the Garden, the Glasshouse and the indoor exhibits. For photographs, the Garden is the best part. Tall glass towers in strong colours stand among the plants, and the Space Needle rises behind them. The Citron Icicle Tower is a good one to line up, either silhouetted or lit against the Needle. The big glass globes also pick up bent, coloured reflections of the tower, which makes a different kind of picture. Inside the Glasshouse, a suspended sculpture about 100 feet (around 30 metres) long is one of Chihuly's largest, and it fills the space overhead. Through the glass wall you can frame the colourful sculpture with the Space Needle outside. Move around before you shoot, because a small step sideways changes how the tower and the Needle overlap. Keep your phone about 12 inches (30 cm) from any glass, and leave the flash off. Tripods and selfie sticks are not allowed in the galleries. The site is admission-only, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Seattle Center, directly next to the Space Needle, on the site of the former Fun Forest.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so head for Seattle Center, the large public campus around the Space Needle. Once inside Seattle Center, the garden entrance is right beside the Space Needle, so walk towards the tower and look for the glass building and garden next to it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the glass towers with the Space Needle behind them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the big suspended sculpture overhead in the Glasshouse. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out one tower or one globe.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here one of the tall glass towers sits against the Space Needle, silhouetted or lit. The Needle is the backdrop, and the tower is the subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the tower off-centre and let the Space Needle rise behind it. Turn on gridlines to keep the Needle upright. For a second picture, crouch beside one of the large glass spheres and frame the Needle's reflection, which is bent and coloured inside the glass. Inside, stand under the glass sculpture and shoot up through the glass wall, with the Space Needle outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glass tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the colours stay rich. If the glass looks washed out, lower it a bit more. Keep the phone about 12 inches (30 cm) from glass, and leave the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Opening hours vary, so check before you go. Soft, low light, such as late afternoon, usually makes glass colours look richer than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: This is an admission-only museum and garden, so check the official site for current hours and entry before you go.

name: Museum of Pop Culture
label: Museum of Pop Culture
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Seattle Center' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Seattle Center' (way/161609433): middle (57 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/161587742: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'MoPOP: Museum of Pop Culture' (131 m across).

text.description: The Museum of Pop Culture is a nonprofit museum dedicated to contemporary popular culture. Paul Allen founded it in 2000 as the Experience Music Project, and it took its current name in November 2016. The building was designed by Frank O. Gehry and covers about 140,000 square feet (13,000 m²). From the outside it looks like a heap of folded, curving metal in several colours, and that is what makes it easy to photograph on a phone. Stand back far enough to take in the whole curving shape, then walk closer and photograph the panels alone. The colours and curves change a lot as you move, so try a few positions. If you want a portrait, the purple panels on the west side make a strong backdrop behind a person. Early or late in the day the colour looks richest. On a clear day the reflections are at their strongest. Only the outside is covered here. Rules for taking photos inside vary by exhibit, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum sits on the Seattle Center campus in Seattle, right next to the Space Needle.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is given for this spot; head to Seattle Center, the campus beside the Space Needle. Walk across the grounds towards the curving metal building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building and the Space Needle into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for cleaner, less stretched views of the panels. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for close-ups of the panel patterns and colours.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Seattle Center (grounds beside the museum, toward the Space Needle). The museum's reflective panels with the Space Needle in the same frame, including reflections of the tower and the campus greenery. On the Space Needle side of the museum, with the building to the east of you. From here the shiny panels show the tower and the campus trees reflected in them, so you can get the Space Needle in the same shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the Space Needle and its reflection off-centre. Tilt the phone slightly upwards so the curves of the building sweep across the frame. For a different shot, stand close to the purple panels on the west side and use portrait mode with a person in front of them. Moving a few steps changes the angles and colours a lot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest panel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours do not wash out and the reflections stay visible. Take a few shots, since the metal can look different from step to step.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A clear day gives the strongest reflections. Low sun at sunrise or sunset, or late afternoon, brings out the colour of the panels, so check the light on the day.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the open Seattle Center grounds without paying admission; for the inside, check the official site before you go, as photo rules vary by exhibit.

name: Seattle Aquarium
label: Seattle Aquarium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pier 62' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pier 62' (way/57391649): middle (152 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16051213: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Seattle Aquarium' (192 m across).

text.description:
The Seattle Aquarium sits on the Elliott Bay waterfront, with its original buildings on Pier 59 and Pier 60. It opened on 20 May 1977, and a newer building, the Ocean Pavilion, opened in August 2024. That building has a yellow cedar exterior designed to look like driftwood, and artwork by Lummi artist Dan Friday on the outside. It is a good subject because the water, the aquarium buildings and the city all fit into one frame.

The best everyday view is from Pier 62, just along the waterfront. From the north end of the pier you look back across the water to the aquarium on Pier 59. The Seattle skyline and the Great Wheel sit close by, so one photo can show the aquarium, the water and the city together. If you want a second angle, the Overlook Walk gives a higher view down onto the Pier 59 building and the Great Wheel. Pier 66 gives a wider downtown-and-shoreline view that still takes in the aquarium.

Keep the building as your main subject and let the wheel and skyline sit behind it. Keep the phone level so the pier edge and waterline stay straight. Wipe your lens first, because sea air and fingerprints soften a photo. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, since the pier is open and you can easily step sideways to change the angle.
text.geographic_location: On the central Seattle waterfront on Elliott Bay, on Pier 59 and Pier 60 next to the Great Wheel. The new waterfront promenade includes an overpass linking it to Pike Place Market.
text.directions_text: Head for the central Seattle waterfront, near Pike Place Market, and make for Pier 62, which is just north-west of the aquarium. If you are coming from further away, head to the central waterfront near the aquarium and walk to Pier 62. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the aquarium, skyline and Great Wheel in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the aquarium from across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pier 62 (north end of the pier, looking back toward the aquarium). The aquarium building on Pier 59 seen across the water from the open pier, with the Seattle skyline and the Great Wheel nearby. From here the aquarium building on Pier 59 lies to the south-east across the water. With the skyline and the Great Wheel nearby, you can include all of them in one photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the aquarium on one third of the frame, with the skyline or the Great Wheel on another. Include a strip of water in the foreground to give depth. For a different view, the Overlook Walk looks down on the building and the wheel, and Pier 66 gives a wider shoreline shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the aquarium building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building and the water keep their detail. Try a panorama along the pier edge, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the afternoon or early evening, when the sun is likely behind you and lights the aquarium side of the view. Early morning is usually quieter on the pier.

text.access_note: Pier 62 is an open waterfront space, but entry to the aquarium itself is likely ticketed, so check the aquarium's website before you go for tickets, opening times and any waterfront closures or construction.

text.description: T-Mobile Park is the home of the Seattle Mariners baseball team, and it has a retractable roof and room for 47,368 spectators. The first game here was played on 15 July 1999. It was called Safeco Field until the name changed on 1 January 2019. It sits in the SoDo district, just south of Lumen Field, and from up close it is a huge, hard-to-fit building. The best phone picture is therefore the long view from Dr. From the hillside you look down over the stadium, with the city, Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains around it. It is a quieter, higher alternative to street-level shots. The stadium will look fairly small in the frame, so think of it as part of a wide Seattle scene rather than the only subject. If you would rather be close, the stadium's main gate has two Mariners bronze statues in front, and The MITT, a giant bronze baseball mitt sculpture, makes a fun foreground. Both can be busy on game days, and sculptures and crowd barriers may change, so look at the spot when you arrive. The best views from inside the ground need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: T-Mobile Park is in the SoDo district, just south of downtown Seattle, with Lumen Field directly to its north. Jose Rizal Park, to the east of the stadium.
text.directions_text: Dr. Jose Rizal Park is on Beacon Hill, east of the stadium, so check the route on the map. For the main gate and statues, head to the stadium itself in SoDo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the city, water and mountains. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the stadium closer. Avoid the ultra-wide (0.5x) here, because it will make the stadium tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dr. Jose Rizal Park (Beacon Hill hillside viewpoint looking down over the stadium). A distant, elevated view of the stadium alongside the city, Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains. Stand on Dr. From here you look down over the stadium, with the city, Puget Sound and the Olympic Mountains beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the stadium on a lower third line, leaving the skyline, water and mountains in the upper part. Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot so you have both the whole scene and a closer look at the ballpark. If you prefer a close-up, the main gate with its two Mariners statues, or The MITT with the stadium wall behind it, are good alternatives at street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and detailed. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in. Panorama mode can work well for the sweep from the city to the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day so the distant mountains show. Looking west, morning sun is behind you and lights the stadium, while evening sun will be in front of you and can make shots darker or glarey.

text.access_note: Dr. Jose Rizal Park is a public park; the stadium itself is ticketed for games and events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west from Beacon Hill, the morning sun is behind the viewer and the evening sun is in front.
Clear days give the best visibility of the Olympic Mountains.
From the viewpoint the stadium will look fairly small in the frame, so zooming helps.

name: Kerry Park
label: Kerry Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kerry Park' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/49734702: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kerry Park' (99 m across).
notes: Classic skyline view with the Space Needle and Mount Rainier.

text.description: Kerry Park is a small public park on the south slope of Queen Anne Hill, and it is one of the best-known places in Seattle to photograph the city. The railing and benches face south, so downtown fills the view, with the Space Needle near the centre, Elliott Bay to the west and, on a clear day, Mount Rainier in the distance. The park covers about 1.26 acres and was given to the city in 1927 by Albert and Katharine Kerry, who lived nearby, so that anyone who stopped here could enjoy the view. In the middle stands Changing Form, a 15-foot (4.6 m) steel sculpture installed in 1971. It is hollow, and photographers use it as a frame for the skyline. The classic spot is along the railing, but the right-hand side of the park, up on the dirt mound, gives a fuller skyline angle with less shrubbery in the way and no railing in the picture. Because the park is small and the view is famous, expect other people at the railing, especially around sunset. Be patient, wait for a gap, and then take several shots. Keep your phone steady against your body and check the horizon is level before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: Kerry Park is on West Highland Drive, between 2nd Avenue West and 3rd Avenue West, on the south side of Queen Anne Hill. It looks over Downtown Seattle.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Queen Anne area of Seattle and make your way to West Highland Drive, between 2nd Avenue West and 3rd Avenue West. A stairway at the west end of the park links it with West Prospect Street below, if you are arriving on foot from that side. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full skyline. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the sculpture and the city together, and try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Space Needle or Mount Rainier.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, the railing and the downtown skyline with the Space Needle are in front of you. For a fuller skyline angle with less shrubbery in the way, walk a short way to the right to the dirt mound.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the skyline along the upper third, with the lawn and railing leading the eye in from below. For a different picture, go to Changing Form and frame the Space Needle through or behind the sculpture's shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the buildings do not wash out. Keep the phone level using the gridlines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset usually suits a south-facing view, but the park is busier then. Clear days are the best for seeing Mount Rainier.

text.access_note: Kerry Park is a public park, but one visitor reported part of the lower area closed for tree pruning, so check conditions before you go.

name: Seattle Central Library
label: Central Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '4th Ave and Spring St corner' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of 4th Avenue and Spring Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37056442: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Seattle Central Library' (133 m across).
notes: Glass and steel library designed by Rem Koolhaas.

text.description: Seattle Central Library is the main library of the Seattle Public Library system, and it looks like nothing else on the street. The 11-storey glass and steel building opened on 23 May 2004 and stands about 57 metres (185 feet) tall. It was designed by Rem Koolhaas and Joshua Prince-Ramus of OMA, working with the Seattle firm LMN Architects. The building looks like several 'floating platforms' wrapped in a steel net around a glass skin. That net is what makes it such a good phone subject: the diamond grid of the glass facade repeats across the whole front, and the angled forms catch the sky and change as the light moves. There are nearly 10,000 custom-sized windows, so the pattern is everywhere you point your phone. It is the third library on this block, which is bounded by Fourth and Fifth Avenues and Madison and Spring Streets. The 4th Ave and Spring St corner, a short walk north along the same side, is another viewpoint worth trying. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the building does not look as if it is leaning. If you have time, the Fourth Avenue and Madison Street corner shows the tower rising above the intersection, and Freeway Park frames it with trees in the foreground. Tripods are not allowed inside, so plan to shoot handheld.
text.geographic_location: The library is in the downtown core of Seattle, on the block bounded by Fourth and Fifth Avenues and Madison and Spring Streets, at 1000 Fourth Avenue.
text.directions_text: From here the middle of the building is to the east, about 1 minute on foot. The corner of Fourth Avenue and Spring Street is a nearby alternative viewpoint, a short walk north along the same side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a head-on shot of the diamond grid. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole tower will not fit from the pavement. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of 4th Avenue and Spring Street. The library's diamond-grid glass facade seen head-on from the street corner. From here you look at the library's glass facade head-on, which gives the sharpest view of the diamond grid. The building is to the east of you. The 4th Ave and Spring St corner is a separate viewpoint a short walk north along the same side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's edges. Hold the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it up makes the sides lean inwards. For a closer pattern shot, zoom in on a section of the grid and let it fill the frame. For a different view, try the 4th Ave and Spring St corner, the Fourth Avenue and Madison Street corner, or Freeway Park, where trees frame the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the glass to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the grid. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post, not a tripod.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Aim for 9-11 am or dusk, which a travel guide recommends as the best light for this view.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public pavement, but check the official site before you go for opening hours and photo rules inside, as tripods are not allowed indoors.

name: Gas Works Park
label: Gas Works Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gas Works Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gas Works Park' (relation/1047789): middle (499 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1047789: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gas Works Park' (500 m across).
notes: Former gasification plant with skyline views over Lake Union.

text.description:
Gas Works Park is a 19.1-acre public park on the north shore of Lake Union, built around the remains of a coal gasification plant that ran from 1906 to 1956. Seattle bought the site in 1962 and the park opened in 1975, designed by landscape architect Richard Haag. It is also the only surviving plant of its kind in the United States. Some of the old machinery stands as rusted ruins, and other parts have been painted and reused in the children's play barn.

From here the downtown towers and the Space Needle sit on the far side of the lake. The dark industrial structures fill one side of the frame, and seaplanes and boats often add movement on the water. It is the mix of old industry and city skyline that makes this view different from other viewpoints in Seattle. A sundial is built into the summit, which gives you something to place in the foreground.

A second view worth trying has Lake Union in the foreground and the towers as dark silhouettes at blue hour. Keep to the public paths, because some of the rusted structures are fenced off, and do not climb the towers. The lake water is contaminated, so stay out of it.
text.geographic_location: Gas Works Park is on the north shore of Lake Union, at the south end of the Wallingford neighbourhood. It sits on a promontory between the lake's northwest and northeast arms.
text.directions_text: From the Wallingford neighbourhood, head south towards the Lake Union shore to the park address, 2101 N Northlake Way, Seattle, WA 98103. Parking lots near Northlake Way fill quickly on summer evenings, so allow extra time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole skyline across the lake. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Space Needle and towers closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the rusted structures close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Gas Works Park (top of the grassy hill (Kite Hill), facing south across Lake Union toward downtown). Downtown towers and the Space Needle across the lake, with the rusted plant structures on one side and seaplanes and boats on the water. At the top of the grassy hill (Kite Hill), facing south across Lake Union. Guides disagree on the best spot on the hilltop, so walk around the lawn a little before you settle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line. Let the rusted structures fill one side of the frame to give depth, with the skyline on the other. For a different angle, try the view with Lake Union in the foreground and the towers as dark silhouettes. Keep the sundial or the grass in the lower part of the frame if you want a foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour at sunset. At blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows against your body so the phone stays still. Use panorama sparingly, because moving boats and seaplanes can come out oddly stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and blue hour are the most recommended times, when the sky colours and the city lights start to come on.

text.access_note: This is an open public park, but some of the rusted structures are fenced off, and fireworks or events can close parts of the park on some dates, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the hilltop facing south, the sunset happens off to your right (west).
Seaplanes and boats are often on the water, so they add movement to the view.
Resting your elbows against your body helps keep a phone steady in night mode.
The hilltop is reached by an easy walk up grass.

name: Volunteer Park
label: Volunteer Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Black Sun' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Black Sun' (node/772402830): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13800188: large area 'Volunteer Park' (628 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Capitol Hill park with a water tower viewpoint and conservatory.

text.description: Volunteer Park is a large, leafy park on a ridge in Capitol Hill, and it is the place for a classic Seattle photo: the Space Needle seen through the round hole of Isamu Noguchi's Black Sun sculpture, which locals call "The Doughnut". The sculpture sits across from the Seattle Asian Art Museum, so the Art Deco museum is close by if you want a second shot. The park covers about 48 acres. The city bought the land in 1876, and in 1903 the Olmsted Brothers were brought in to design it as the centrepiece of Seattle's park system. The brick water tower dates from 1906 and the Victorian-style glass conservatory from 1912. The museum building went up in 1932 as the original Seattle Art Museum. Beyond the sculpture there are wide lawns, tree-lined paths and a dahlia garden in season, so you can fill a roll of photos here without hurrying. The Space Needle is a long way off, so it will look small in the frame, but that is what makes the picture work: the sculpture becomes a dark ring around it. Take a few shots with slightly different positions, because a small step sideways changes how the Needle sits in the hole. For variety, the conservatory with the Seward statue in front of it makes a good traditional shot. The water tower has views from its observation deck, but that deck keeps posted hours, so check before you go.
text.geographic_location: Volunteer Park is in the Capitol Hill neighbourhood of Seattle, on a ridge near downtown. The Black Sun sculpture stands across from the Seattle Asian Art Museum inside the park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check current local transport options before you go and head for Volunteer Park in Capitol Hill. Once inside, look for the Seattle Asian Art Museum; Black Sun is across from it. The park is large, so treat that as an approximate map location only: the sculpture itself, across from the museum, is the viewpoint to look for. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see how the Space Needle sits inside the hole, then try telephoto (2x or 3x) to bring the Needle closer and fill more of the opening. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the museum or the wide lawns, not for this shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (across from the Seattle Asian Art Museum, looking through the sculpture's central hole). The Space Needle framed inside the donut-shaped hole of the Black Sun sculpture. Across from the Seattle Asian Art Museum, and look through the sculpture's central hole. The Space Needle should appear framed inside the donut-shaped opening. Move a step or two left or right until the Needle sits neatly in the middle of the ring.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and use them to centre the Needle in the opening. Hold the phone steady and close to the sculpture so the ring forms a clean border. Try one shot in portrait orientation and one in landscape. If you have time, the conservatory with the Seward statue in front of it is a good second subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Space Needle to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the dark sculpture does not wash out the picture. Tap again if the phone refocuses on the sculpture instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend morning. Check the light on the day, as haze can hide the Needle.

text.access_note: The park is an open public space; the water tower's observation deck has posted hours and the conservatory asks for permission for formal shoots, so check the official site before you go.

name: Seattle Great Wheel
label: Seattle Great Wheel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pier 57' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pier 57' (relation/812609): middle (182 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1809238334: the OpenStreetMap point 'Seattle Great Wheel'.

text.description:
The Seattle Great Wheel is a 53-metre (175 ft) Ferris wheel on Pier 57, beside Elliott Bay. It opened in June 2012 and was then the tallest Ferris wheel on the West Coast of the United States. It is also the only wheel of its design in North America built out over water. The ride extends about 12 metres beyond the pier's edge, and the 42 enclosed gondolas carry riders through three turns in around 12 minutes.

It photographs well because the pier gives you the wheel in the foreground, with the downtown skyline and the water of Elliott Bay behind it. This is the angle most visitors choose. The big circle gives a simple, strong shape, and the spokes and gondolas add detail when you stand close.

If you want a different view, Pier 62 shows the wheel against the water and skyline, and it is a good place to see the lit wheel reflected on the bay after dark. Jose Rizal Park gives a more distant view, with trees framing the city and the wheel among the buildings.

For steady pictures, stay on the outdoor pier. Glass reflections make shots from inside the gondolas difficult. The wheel's hours can change, so check the current schedule on the day.
text.geographic_location: The Seattle Great Wheel stands at the end of Pier 57 on Elliott Bay in Seattle. The city skyline rises behind it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so head to Pier 57 on Elliott Bay in Seattle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wheel with the skyline and bay behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole wheel in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the gondolas or the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pier 57 (end of the pier, where the wheel stands). The wheel in the foreground with the downtown skyline and Elliott Bay behind it. From here your photo shows the wheel in the foreground with the downtown skyline and Elliott Bay behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the wheel on one side of the frame, with the skyline and water filling the rest. Hold the phone level so the wheel stays round and the horizon straight. For a different view, try Pier 62 for the wheel against the water and skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wheel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays rich and the lights don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a rail for a steadier shot. Don't shoot through gondola windows, as reflections spoil the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good choice, as the wheel's lights show against the sky and the bay. Check the current schedule before you go.

text.access_note: The pier viewpoint is free to visit, but hours and ride access can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Olympic Sculpture Park
label: Olympic Sculpture Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eagle' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Seattle Eagle' (way/434703405): middle (29 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7406606: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Olympic Sculpture Park' (427 m across).
notes: Waterfront sculpture park with views of Elliott Bay.

text.description:
Olympic Sculpture Park is a free outdoor sculpture park run by the Seattle Art Museum. It sits on a 9-acre site beside Puget Sound, and it was once an industrial site. It opened on 20 January 2007.

For a phone photo, the best-known piece is Eagle (1971) by Alexander Calder. It is a tall, bold, orange-red steel sculpture with simple curved shapes. From its west side you can line it up with the Space Needle in the distance, so the sculpture frames the skyline. Two other pieces are worth a quick shot if you have time. Echo, a tall white head by Jaume Plensa, works well with the Sound and sky behind it. Wake, by Richard Serra, is a group of weathered steel walls that make good abstract pictures from different angles.

The museum has a no-touch policy to protect the artworks, so don't climb on or lean against them. Eagle's paint was fully renewed in 2020, so it should look crisp. Evening is the most rewarding time, when the colours warm up and the steel stands out against the sky. Check the official site before you go for opening times and any closures.
text.geographic_location: The park is in Belltown, in downtown Seattle, at the northern end of the Central Waterfront. It sits next to Myrtle Edwards Park, on the shore of Puget Sound.
text.directions_text: Head for Belltown, at the northern end of the Central Waterfront, and look for the park beside Myrtle Edwards Park on the water's edge. Once inside, walk to Eagle, the large orange-red sculpture, and go round to its west side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for Eagle and the Space Needle together. Use the default lens (1x) for Echo against the Sound and sky. A telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) suits close-up abstract shots of Wake.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (west side of the Calder sculpture, looking toward the Space Needle). Calder's orange steel sculpture in the foreground framing the Space Needle, with a wide-angle lens from the west side. Walk to the west side of Calder's Eagle inside the park. From there you are looking towards the Space Needle, with the orange-red steel of Eagle in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place Eagle's big shape on one side of the frame, leaving the Space Needle in the open space beyond. Crouch low and tilt the phone up so the red steel cuts into the sky. If you want a different view, try Echo with the water and sky behind it, or Wake from several angles for abstract shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Space Needle or the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the sculpture doesn't wash out. At sunset, check that the Space Needle hasn't turned into a silhouette you didn't want.

text.access_note: This is a free, open public park, but check the official site before you go for opening times and closures, and for any rules on commercial photography.
claims_not_in_sources: Getting low and tilting the phone up makes a tall sculpture break into the sky more dramatically (general framing advice; one guide suggests this for Eagle at sunset).
An ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps fit a large foreground sculpture and a distant landmark into one frame.
Echo and Wake are in the park but their exact positions are approximate, so the photo spots for them are not pinned precisely on the map.

name: Fremont Troll
label: Fremont Troll
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Troll Knoll Forest' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Troll's Knoll Park' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2485251324: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fremont Troll'.
notes: Giant troll sculpture under the Aurora Bridge.

text.description: The Fremont Troll is a huge concrete sculpture crouched under the north end of the Aurora Bridge (the George Washington Memorial Bridge), on N 36th Street at Troll Avenue N. It stands 18 ft (5.5 m) high and is made of steel rebar, wire and concrete. In one hand it clutches a real Volkswagen Beetle with a California licence plate, as if it had just grabbed it from the road above. It photographs well because the scale is easy to read and the details are fun: the hubcap eye, the shaggy hair and the car. Four artists made it in 1990, drawing on the Scandinavian folklore of a troll living under a bridge. From here you can frame the troll with the garden's greenery and its moss turtle, which makes a calmer picture than the busy street-level view. Take a few shots from the garden, then walk down to the street for the classic full-length frame with the bridge overhead. The area sits under a busy bridge, so keep out of the traffic lanes and watch for no-parking signs if you arrive by car. If you want to climb on the sculpture, follow any signs on site and use your own judgement.
text.geographic_location: In the Fremont district of Seattle, directly under the north end of the Aurora Bridge, where N 36th Street meets Troll Avenue N.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Fremont and go by taxi or hired scooter to the corner of N 36th Street and Troll Avenue N, under the north end of the Aurora Bridge. From there the troll is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the garden to include the troll and the greenery around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer and want the troll and the bridge above in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the face and the Beetle.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Troll Knoll Forest (The garden beside the troll; reviewers mention the little park to its right). The troll framed with the garden's greenery and its moss turtle, a softer and less crowded alternative to the street-level frame. The garden beside the troll. The troll is just to the south-west of you. From here you can frame it with the garden's greenery and the moss turtle, a softer and usually less crowded view than the street-level frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the troll's head and hand on one of the lines, with some plants in the foreground. For the full 18 ft figure with the bridge overhead, go down to street level. Another good view is along Troll Avenue North, framed by the concrete bridge supports with the troll behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the troll's face to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky behind washes out the concrete. If people walk through, take a few Live Photos or a short burst and pick the clearest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight, and try a weekday or early in the day, because weekends can be crowded and you may have to wait for a clear frame.

text.access_note: The troll stands in an open public space under a busy bridge, so stay out of the traffic lanes; check the official site and any signs on site before you go, especially about climbing.

name: Smith Tower
label: Smith Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Occidental Square' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Occidental Square' (way/174692555): middle (102 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/52781661: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Smith Tower' (67 m across).

text.description:
Smith Tower stands in the Pioneer Square neighbourhood and is one of the easiest Seattle buildings to pick out in a photo, thanks to its pyramid-shaped crown. It was completed in 1914 at 38 storeys and 462 ft (141 m), and at the time it was among the tallest skyscrapers outside New York City. It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until 1931, and the tallest on the US West Coast until the Space Needle overtook it in 1962. It is named after Lyman Cornelius Smith, the firearm and typewriter businessman who started the project, and it became a Seattle landmark in 1984.

The best photo here shows the whole tower in its setting, not just the building. That mix of old brick streets and a tall classical tower is what makes the shot work. Golden hour gives the warmest light. If you have time for a second angle, Yesler Way gives a wide view of the tower rising above a parking garage, with reflections in the wet pavement after rain.
text.geographic_location: Smith Tower is in the Pioneer Square neighbourhood of downtown Seattle, at the north-east corner of Yesler Way and Second Avenue. Occidental Square, where you take the photo, is a short walk to the south-west in the same neighbourhood.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Pioneer Square, the neighbourhood around the tower. Occidental Square is a square within Pioneer Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the crown, the buildings and the green space of the square in one frame. If you want just the pyramid top, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone). Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for Yesler Way or when you walk closer to the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Occidental Square. The tower's pyramid crown rising over the historic Pioneer Square streetscape, framed by the square's green space. The tower's pyramid crown rises over the Pioneer Square streetscape, with the square's green space as your foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the crown in the top third. Use trees or the edge of the green space as a frame at the bottom or side, and keep your phone level so the tower's edges stay straight. For a different view, Yesler Way gives a wide-angle shot of the tower above a parking garage. After rain, the wet pavement adds reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower's brightest face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the pale crown keeps its detail. Take a few shots, because people will walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low, warm light falls on the streetscape and the tower.

text.access_note: Occidental Square is an open public space, but the tower's observation deck is a paid attraction, so check the official site before you go if you want to go up.

name: Columbia Center
label: Columbia Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jose Rizal Bridge' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jose Rizal Bridge' (way/368833767): middle (55 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107124288: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Columbia Center' (136 m across).
notes: Tallest building in Seattle with the Sky View Observatory.

text.description:
Columbia Center is the tallest building in Washington state: 76 storeys and 933 ft (284 m), finished in 1985. It is easy to pick out in the Seattle skyline because its three tall faces curve inwards and step back twice, so it looks like three towers standing side by side. The base is clad in Rosa Purino Carnelian granite, but from a distance you will mostly see the glass shaft rising above the other downtown offices.

This map's viewpoint is on Jose Rizal Bridge, south-east of downtown. From here you are looking across the city towards the towers, so Columbia Center will be one tall shape among others rather than a close-up. A skyline list names the bridge as a quieter alternative to Kerry Park, but it does not confirm how well the tower is framed from here, so check the view on the spot. Kerry Park is the better-known alternative, with the downtown skyline, the Space Needle and Elliott Bay, and Mount Rainier on clear days.

For your phone, treat this as a distance shot. Use the telephoto lens to pick the tower out from its neighbours, keep the horizon level with the gridlines, and leave space around the top so it does not feel cramped. If you want to see the city from inside the tower, there is a public observatory on the 73rd floor. Check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Columbia Center stands in downtown Seattle, on the block bounded by Fourth and Fifth Avenues and Cherry and Columbia Streets.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from downtown Seattle at the foot of Columbia Center and head south-east towards Jose Rizal Bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. The default lens (1x) will make it look small and lost among the other buildings. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the bridge and the sky as part of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jose Rizal Bridge. A skyline photo across the city from the bridge; the source does not confirm that Columbia Center is well framed from it. From here the tower is to the north-west, across the city. This is a skyline view of downtown, so find a spot on the bridge where nothing blocks your view of the towers, and look for Columbia Center as the tallest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level so the tall towers do not seem to lean. Place Columbia Center slightly off-centre with some sky above it. Because the framing from the bridge is not confirmed, take a few test shots first and move along the bridge if another building gets in the way. If you want the classic skyline with the Space Needle, try Kerry Park instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. At the longer zoom settings, hold the phone with both hands and press the shutter gently to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the towers. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to steady the phone while the city lights come on.

text.access_note: Jose Rizal Bridge is the viewpoint on this map. The Sky View Observatory in the tower itself is a public observation deck that may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the bridge the tower is seen at a distance among other downtown buildings, so the telephoto lens helps.
Morning light falls on the city from behind a photographer looking north-west from the bridge, and late afternoon light is softer.
City lights come on at dusk, so night mode is useful.
The Sky View Observatory may be ticketed.

name: Lumen Field
label: Lumen Field
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza' (way/1276258884): middle (137 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5838734: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lumen Field' (379 m across).
notes: Home of the Seahawks and Sounders.

text.description: Lumen Field is the big open-air stadium in Seattle's SoDo neighbourhood, home to the Seattle Seahawks, Seattle Sounders FC and Seattle Reign FC. It was built between 2000 and 2002 on the site of the old Kingdome and has taken its current name from a 2020 rebrand of its naming sponsor. For NFL games it holds 68,740 people, so it is a very large structure to fit into a phone screen. The best exterior view is from Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza on the north side. From here the stadium's arches rise overhead, and on game days the crowds stream towards the entrance in front of you. That movement and colour make the picture feel alive, and the arches give you a strong shape to build the frame around. The stadium is a fan favourite for its noise as well as its looks: Seahawks fans twice claimed the Guinness World Record for the loudest crowd roar at an outdoor stadium, in 2013 and 2014. Crowds depend on events, so check the calendar. If you want a different view, Dr. Jose Rizal Park gives a skyline picture of downtown with Lumen Field among the landmarks. Tickets are only needed for events inside the stadium, so the outside views cost nothing.
text.geographic_location: Lumen Field is in the SoDo neighbourhood, within a mile (1.6 km) of Downtown Seattle.
text.directions_text: Head south from Downtown Seattle into SoDo (about a mile). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the arches overhead and the crowd below. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Muckleshoot Heritage Plaza (north side of the stadium). Lumen Field's arches and entrance crowds in the foreground, with the stadium framing the approach on game days. The stadium lies to the south of you, with its arches and the entrance crowds in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arches up with the top third of the frame. Keep the crowd or the entrance path in the foreground so the picture has depth. If you would like a skyline view instead, Dr. Jose Rizal Park is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the arches to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue. On game days, try a Live Photo to capture the crowd moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: On game days the crowds streaming to the entrance add atmosphere. Crowds depend on events, so check the stadium's event calendar before you go.

text.access_note: The plaza outside the stadium is the viewing spot, but entry to the stadium itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The plaza is outdoors and can be reached without a ticket.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky from washing out in this view.

name: Waterfall Garden Park
label: Waterfall Garden Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Waterfall Garden Park' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Main Street and 2nd Avenue South (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/57883614: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Waterfall Garden' (38 m across).
notes: Hidden pocket park with a 22-foot waterfall.

text.description:
Waterfall Garden Park is a small private pocket park in Pioneer Square, made in 1978 at the original United Parcel Service building. It is only about 18 by 24 metres, so it feels like a surprise tucked between city buildings. The star is a man-made waterfall, 22 feet (6.7 m) tall, with a lot of water pumped over it every minute. Around it is a Japanese-style garden with plants native to Japan and a pool, and the park won an environmental award in 1981.

It photographs well because of the contrast: green planting and falling water set against tall buildings. From there you shoot in through the tall gate, which frames a glimpse of the green interior and gives a quieter, more intimate picture than the full waterfall. Many people walk past this entrance without noticing it, so the gate makes an unusual frame. If you step inside, the full cascade, with its potted plants, ornamental trees and tables, is the other classic view.

The space is small, so keep to the paths and don't block other visitors. Small-scale photography needs no permission, but commercial shoots do. Check how the gate framing looks on the spot and adjust your position.
text.geographic_location: In Pioneer Square, Seattle, at the corner of Main and Second. It sits beside the original United Parcel Service building.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to reach the Main and Second corner in Pioneer Square. Once you reach the entrance gateway, the garden and its waterfall are to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) at the gate so the frame of the gateway and the green beyond sit naturally. Inside, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit the waterfall and the buildings above it. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the water or a planting detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Main Street and 2nd Avenue South (the entrance gateway at the sidewalk, shooting in through the tall gate toward the waterfall). A glimpse of the garden's green interior and the sound of falling water framed by the entrance gate, a quieter, more intimate scene than the full waterfall. Stand on Waterfall Garden Park's entrance gateway at the sidewalk, in line with the tall gate, and shoot in towards the waterfall. You will see a glimpse of the green interior framed by the gate, with the sound of falling water. The full cascade is to the north-west, a short walk from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the gate opening in the middle of the frame, with the greenery filling it. Keep the phone level so the gate's edges stay straight. For a second option, step into the garden and shoot the full cascade with the potted plants and tables in the foreground, and the tall buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the green leaves to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky or the white water looks washed out. Try a Live Photo to capture the movement of the water, and hold the phone steady against the gate frame or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the garden is open. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day or in the morning usually keeps the contrast between the shaded garden and the sky under control.

text.access_note: The park is privately owned but open to the public during the day and locked at night, so check the posted hours or the official site before you go.
